analysis.one_liner: Adds a small tax on each stock, bond, and derivatives trade, rising to 0.1%, paid by exchanges and brokers.
analysis.headline: The bill to tax Wall Street trades was introduced on June 18, 2025 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the tax code to impose a tax of 0.02% on the value of each trade of stocks, bonds, partnership interests, and derivatives, rising in steps to 0.1% after 2029. The tax is collected by the exchanges or brokers handling the trade, and it excludes new issues of securities, short-term debt, insurance contracts, and some ordinary business hedging. It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action has been taken.
analysis.who_benefits: The bill's stated purpose is to raise revenue from high-volume trading; the proceeds would be available for federal spending of any kind, and the tax itself falls most heavily on large financial firms, hedge funds, and high-frequency traders rather than on ordinary investors who buy and hold [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal programs funded by new tax revenue

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises revenue from high-volume securities and derivatives trading, which is concentrated among large financial firms and the wealthiest households.

The tax rate phases in gradually, starting at 0.02% and reaching 0.1% after 2029, and exempts the initial issuance of stocks, bonds, and partnership interests so that companies raising capital for investment are not taxed.

analysis.who_pays: The tax is collected and paid by exchanges and brokers on US-connected trades in stocks, bonds, partnership interests, and derivatives, including those involving controlled foreign corporations; the cost can be passed to trading customers, whose trading costs would rise slightly, and some of the burden may reach retirement savers through fund managers [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Big trading firms and their customers

drawbacks.text: The tax is levied on the exchange or broker, which can pass costs to customers through wider spreads or higher fees, so some of the cost could reach ordinary investors with retirement accounts.

A tax imposed only on US-connected trading could push some trading activity to foreign exchanges, and Congress.gov's record shows no committee action yet, so there is no evidence of the bipartisan support such a bill would need to pass.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a real revenue stream raised mostly from high-volume trading, with small direct cost to ordinary households; the drawback is that traders may pass some tax through via wider spreads, and a US-only tax could push some trading overseas. But the tax rate is phased in slowly and exempts initial stock and bond issues, so the design avoids the sharpest pass-through and market-making risks cited by critics.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, and no vote or further action has ever been taken on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 18, 2025 and, the same day, was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The action history shows no hearings, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action after the referral.

The bill sits on the Senate calendar-in-waiting only in the sense of having been referred; its sponsor is a Democrat and all five cosponsors are Democrats [S3], and the Senate Finance Committee has not taken it up.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-volume Wall Street trading firms and the exchanges and brokers that profit from that volume are better off, because the tax never advanced and they will not pay it. The potential revenue it would have raised for public priorities was never collected.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Chris Van Hollen, Sheldon Whitehouse, John Fetterman, and Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors.

against.name: Financial services industry
against.role: Banks, trading firms, and their lobbying groups
against.what_they_did: Financial industry groups have long opposed trading taxes of this kind and lobby against them; the Finance Committee never scheduled any action on this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats [S3]; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-led agenda in the Senate Finance Committee has left the bill untouched [S4].

industries.industry: Banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency trading firms
industries.note: These firms execute enormous volumes of trades, so a per-trade tax falls most heavily on them; they profit from high-volume, low-margin trading. Ordinary retail investors trade far less often and pay proportionally much less.

industries.industry: Stock and derivatives exchanges (NYSE, CME, etc.)
industries.note: Exchanges and brokers are made responsible for collecting and paying the tax on trades they handle. Their trading volumes could fall if the tax discourages trading, though they bear the cost only as collectors.

analysis.trajectory: With all-Democratic sponsorship, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action since referral in June 2025, the bill is very unlikely to reach a floor vote in this Congress; its realistic path is the same as its predecessors: it will sit in committee unless it is attached to a larger tax or reconciliation bill, which is not currently signaled in the record.
